blocks.text: A stack is a linear data structure that only exposes one end, the top. You push elements onto it, you pop elements off it, and the most recently pushed element is always the first one to come back off, the LIFO rule. That part is assumed knowledge here, this document is not about what a stack is or how to implement one from an array or a linked list.

What it is about is recognizing exactly when a problem is quietly asking for a stack, and then implementing the small set of problem patterns that keep showing up once you do. Three signals tend to appear whenever a stack is the right tool:

items: You need to remember something now but only act on it later, in the exact reverse order you encountered it
You need to match up nested or paired structures, an opening element that must eventually be closed by a corresponding closing element
You need to undo or cancel only the single most recent action, never the oldest one

blocks.text: Every pattern below is one of those three signals wearing a different costume. Balanced parentheses is signal two. Removing adjacent duplicates is signal three. Postfix evaluation is signal one. Once you can name which signal a problem is giving off, the stack based solution tends to fall out almost automatically.

content.title: 1. Balanced Parentheses: The Classic Matching Pattern

blocks.text: Given a string made only of the characters (, ), {, }, [, and ], decide whether every opening bracket is closed by the correct type of closing bracket, in the correct order. This is the canonical example of signal two, matching nested structures, and it is almost always the first stack problem anyone sees.

The key realization is that whenever you hit a closing bracket, it must match the most recently opened bracket that has not yet been closed. Not the oldest one, not any earlier one, specifically the most recent one. That phrase, most recent and not yet closed, is exactly what a stack top gives you for free.

items: See an opening bracket, (, {, or [: push it onto the stack
See a closing bracket: if the stack is empty or its top does not match the expected opening bracket, the string is invalid, otherwise pop the stack
After scanning the entire string, the string is valid only if the stack ends up completely empty

blocks.caption: Scanning left to right: opening brackets are pushed, and each closing bracket must match the top of the stack before it can pop.
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406762988-155525955.png
blocks.alt: Balanced Parentheses: The Classic Matching Pattern

blocks.text: That third rule, checking the stack is empty at the very end, is the step almost everyone forgets. A string like ((( passes every single check while it is being scanned, nothing ever mismatches, it only fails because the stack is not empty once the scan is done.

Both the time and the space used by this approach are proportional to the length of the string, each character is pushed at most once and popped at most once, so the algorithm runs in linear time and uses linear extra space in the worst case.

content.title: 2. Worked Example: Tracing a Balanced String

blocks.text: Tracing the algorithm by hand on a small input makes the final emptiness check concrete. Take the string {[()]} and walk through it one character at a time.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Character","Action","Stack (bottom to top)"],"rows":[["1","{","Opening bracket, push","{"],["2","[","Opening bracket, push","{  ["],["3","(","Opening bracket, push","{  [  ("],["4",")","Closing bracket, top is (, matches, pop","{  ["],["5","]","Closing bracket, top is [, matches, pop","{"],["6","}","Closing bracket, top is {, matches, pop","empty"],["7","end of string","Stack is empty, string is valid","empty"]]}

blocks.text: Every single pop found the correct matching opening bracket sitting at the top, and the stack was empty the moment the last character was processed. Both conditions hold, so the string is valid.

Contrast that with a string like {[(])}. By the time the algorithm reaches ), the top of the stack is [, not (. The mismatch is caught immediately and the function returns false right there, it never even needs to look at the remaining characters.

And a string like ((( shows the opposite failure mode: every character pushes cleanly and no mismatch ever fires, the string only fails because three opening brackets are still sitting on the stack when scanning finishes.

content.title: 3. Remove Adjacent Duplicates Using a Stack

blocks.text: Given a string, repeatedly remove any two adjacent characters that are identical, until no such pair remains. This is signal three, undoing the most recent action, the character you just added is exactly the one that gets cancelled the moment an identical character shows up right next to it.

items: For each character in the string: if the stack is not empty and its top equals the current character, pop the stack instead of pushing, this is the cancellation
Otherwise, push the current character onto the stack
After scanning the entire string, the characters remaining in the stack, read from bottom to top, form the final answer

blocks.caption: Matching the top pushes nothing, it pops instead, cancelling the pair that was just formed.
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406762988-419202540.png
blocks.alt: Remove Adjacent Duplicates Using a Stack

blocks.text: Trace it on abbaca: push a, push b, the next b matches the top so pop leaving a, the next a matches the top so pop leaving the stack empty, push c, push a. The stack ends as ca, which is the answer.
Using string with push_back and pop_back is a common trick, a std::string behaves exactly like a stack of characters here, and building the answer this way avoids a separate reversal step at the end.

content.title: 4. The Reverse Order Insight: Call Stacks, Undo, and Back Buttons

blocks.text: Signal one, remembering something now to act on later in reverse order, is not just a coding interview trick, it is how several systems you use every day are actually built underneath.

A browser back button is a stack of visited pages. Every page you navigate to gets pushed. Pressing back pops the most recently visited page, never the oldest one, that is why back always undoes your most recent navigation first.

Undo in a text editor works the same way. Every edit gets pushed onto an undo stack as you make it. Pressing undo pops the most recent edit and reverses it, one step backward through your own history, most recent first.

The most direct example is the actual call stack your programs run on. Every function call pushes a new frame, and when a function returns, its frame is popped and control resumes exactly where the caller left off, at the most recently paused point. Recursion works at all only because the runtime is silently pushing and popping frames for you on every call and return.

This is why the phrase used earlier, remember now and act later in reverse order, is worth memorizing on its own. It is the signal, and a stack is very often the mechanism, whether you reach for one explicitly or the language runtime is already using one on your behalf.

In postfix notation, also called Reverse Polish Notation or RPN, every operator comes after its operands instead of between them. There is no ambiguity about precedence and no need for parentheses at all, the order the tokens appear in already tells you exactly what to do.
The evaluation rule is a direct instance of signal one, remember operands until an operator says it is time to use them, and use the most recently remembered ones first:

items: Scan the expression left to right, one token at a time
If the token is a number, push it onto the stack
If the token is an operator, pop the top two values off the stack, apply the operator, and push the result back on
After the last token, exactly one value remains on the stack, the final result

blocks.text: Order matters the moment the operator is not commutative. For a subtraction token following operands a and b, the second value popped is a and the first value popped is b, so the computation must be a minus b, not b minus a.

blocks.caption: Operands are pushed until an operator pops the two most recent values, applies itself, and pushes the result back.
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406762988-437550573.png
blocks.alt: Evaluating Postfix Expressions Reverse Polish Notation

codes.javascript:
Expression: "2 1 + 3 *"

token "2"   push 2                 stack: [2]
token "1"   push 1                 stack: [2, 1]
token "+"   pop 1, pop 2, push 3   stack: [3]
token "3"   push 3                 stack: [3, 3]
token "*"   pop 3, pop 3, push 9   stack: [9]

Result: 9

content.title: 6. From Postfix to Infix: A Note on Basic Calculator Problems

blocks.text: Postfix expressions are convenient because they never need parentheses or precedence rules, but most problems hand you ordinary infix expressions instead, things like 3+5*2. The same push and pop discipline still applies, it just needs one extra piece of state to track precedence.

A common approach keeps a single stack of accumulated values along with a running current number and the last seen operator. Multiplication and division are applied immediately against the previous number on the stack, since they bind tighter than addition and subtraction, while addition and subtraction are simply pushed as signed values and summed at the very end.
Notice the stack is still doing exactly what it always did, holding onto values so they can be combined later, it is just combined with a small amount of extra bookkeeping for operator precedence.
A handful of mistakes account for most stack bugs in these problems:

items: Popping without checking empty() first, calling top() or pop() on an empty stack is undefined behavior in C++, always guard with an emptiness check

Forgetting the final emptiness check on validity problems like balanced parentheses, a string such as ((( never triggers a mismatch mid scan, it only fails because the stack is not empty once scanning finishes
Swapping operand order on non commutative operators when evaluating postfix expressions, the second value popped is always the left operand
Pushing the wrong thing for balanced parentheses, you push the opening bracket itself so you have something concrete to compare against later, not a placeholder or a count
Assuming a stack based solution when the problem does not actually require reverse order processing, not every nested looking problem needs one

blocks.text: If a bug only shows up on inputs like an empty string, a string of only opening brackets, or a single number with no operators, the cause is almost always a missing emptiness check, either before a pop or at the very end.
Problems that build directly on the patterns covered in this document:

items: Easy Valid Parentheses (LC 20): the exact balanced brackets algorithm from this document
Easy Remove All Adjacent Duplicates In String (LC 1047): the exact push or pop on match algorithm from this document
Medium Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation (LC 150): the exact postfix evaluation algorithm from this document
Medium Basic Calculator II (LC 227): extends postfix style evaluation to a full infix expression with plus, minus, multiply, and divide

blocks.text: Every one of these problems is solvable in a single linear pass with one stack, no fancier data structure is needed once the underlying signal is recognized.
Before moving on, make sure each of the following feels automatic:

items: Can you name which of the three signals, reverse order memory, nested matching, or undo the most recent action, a given problem is showing?
Can you implement balanced parentheses from scratch, including the final emptiness check, in under three minutes?
Can you explain why removing adjacent duplicates pops instead of pushing when the top matches the current character?
Can you evaluate a postfix expression by hand and in code, getting operand order right for subtraction and division?
Do you check for an empty stack before every top() or pop() call?

blocks.text: Once matching, cancelling, remembering for later, and evaluating all feel automatic, most basic stack usage questions become a matter of naming the signal and writing code you have effectively already written before.
